source.title: On progressive sharpening, flat minima and generalisation
source.authors: L. MacDonald; Jack Valmadre; Simon Lucey

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on loss sharpness and generalization, arguing that sharpness is neither necessary nor sufficient for good generalization and that Jacobian norm correlates better. It does not test the magnitude-aware sharpness measure in V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for learning rate, batch size, weight decay, label smoothing, mixup, data augmentation, and SAM. Results cited from prior work are not included as rows. Plot values without textual numbers are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The experiments concern generalization, but none tests a supplied version as stated. Sharpness is the largest loss-Hessian eigenvalue, not V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance. The batch-size experiments stop at training-loss thresholds rather than holding epochs fixed, so they do not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' position: they propose that loss curvature relates to generalization through the input-output Jacobian and report better empirical tracking by Jacobian norm than by ordinary Hessian sharpness. Their account is conditional: the ansatz lacks rigorous general conditions, the bound is not numerically evaluated, and empirical Jacobian tracking has reported exceptions.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments measure loss Hessian sharpness and input-output Jacobian norms against generalization gaps. They do not test the claim’s magnitude-aware weight-perturbation measure or its stated comparison against norm- and margin-based measures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationships vary with learning rate, batch size, architecture, weight decay, label smoothing, and regularization strategy. At the largest learning rate, ResNet18 shows an inverse Jacobian-norm/generalization-gap relationship; the authors report this issue for ResNet18 but not VGG11 in their CIFAR10/CIFAR100 experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Without weight decay, ResNet18 can have near-zero training loss and vanishing Hessian sharpness while retaining a relatively large generalization gap; weight decay improves generalization despite sharper minima.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ordinary loss-Hessian flatness is insufficient to predict generalization across weight-decay settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Across ResNet18 and VGG11 on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, smaller batches generally yield better generalization when training stops at a loss threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size affects generalization even when training duration is determined by reaching a training-loss threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Empirical input-output Jacobian norm generally tracks generalization gaps better than ordinary Hessian sharpness across the tested regularizers, with exceptions at high learning rates and measurement complications under mixup and augmentation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Empirical input-output Jacobian norm is a useful but conditional correlate of generalization across training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: Label smoothing changes progressive sharpening, while long cross-entropy training can make both Hessian sharpness and the softmaxed-model empirical Jacobian norm collapse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss curvature and empirical Jacobian trajectories depend on label smoothing and output saturation.

record.problems: The authors state that Ansatz 3.1 is not mathematically rigorous and that they do not numerically evaluate their generalization bound. Many plotted results lack recoverable numerical values in the supplied text. The reported inverse Jacobian/generalization relationship at the largest learning rate is explained speculatively through local Jacobian variation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numeric row values could be recovered from the supplied flattened figure text. Related regression results in Appendix C.3 report sharpness and Jacobian norms but do not measure generalization gap, so they were omitted.

untested.parts: Paired random-label fitting and natural-label held-out performance under the same architecture and recipe.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects with epochs held fixed, including remedies under matched epoch budgets. Appendix B.2 instead matches a training-loss stopping criterion.
Dropout versus no-dropout held-out error. Removing dropout from VGG11 without a corresponding comparison does not test this.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any version. Its criticism of ordinary flatness does not challenge V7's distinct magnitude-aware measure. T6 reflects the absence of a test or operational use of the supplied versions, despite substantial experiments on related generalization questions.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error as network width increases past the interpolation threshold.
Generalization comparison between adaptive optimizers and SGD.
Large-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
The paper measures ordinary loss sharpness, not magnitude-aware sharpness or tolerance to weight-scaled perturbations.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Train with cross-entropy and varying weight decay; report end-of-training metrics.
rows.measure: Generalization gap (loss), sharpness, and input-output Jacobian norm
rows.baseline: Without weight decay: near-zero loss, vanishing sharpness, and relatively large Jacobian norm and generalization gap.
rows.value: Weight decay varied; figure-only values for individual settings.
rows.note: Authors explicitly report that weight decay improves generalization despite sharper minima; the plot does not provide recoverable numeric values in the supplied text.
rows.check: Ordinary Hessian sharpness and Jacobian norm do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness. The reported weight-decay result is valid but cannot establish a state for any supplied version.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD at differing constant learning rates; report end-of-training metrics.
rows.baseline: Figure-only; varying learning rates and batch sizes are compared.
rows.value: Figure-only; authors state larger learning rates typically have smaller sharpness and generalize better.
rows.uncertainty: Five trials; plotted uncertainty not specified in main text.
rows.locator: Figure 3; Section 6, “Learning rate and batch size”
rows.note: The authors describe the trend as typical, not universal. Numerical values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Appendix B.2 specifies termination when the mean of the latest ten training-loss evaluations falls below 0.01 on CIFAR10, not a fixed epoch budget. Learning-rate effects and Hessian sharpness do not independently test a supplied version.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD using differing batch sizes and constant learning rates; report end-of-training metrics.
rows.baseline: Figure-only; varying batch sizes and learning rates are compared.
rows.value: At smaller learning rates, increasing batch size typically increases sharpness and generalization gap; at the largest learning rate, the reported Jacobian-gap relationship is inverse.
rows.uncertainty: Five trials; plotted uncertainty not specified in main text.
rows.locator: Figure 4; Section 6, “Learning rate and batch size”
rows.note: The text explicitly identifies the inverse Jacobian-norm/generalization-gap relationship at the largest learning rate; precise values are figure-only.
rows.check: Batch sizes are compared at a training-loss stopping criterion, not V5's fixed epoch budget. The measure is the absolute training–test loss gap. The high-learning-rate exception concerns Jacobian tracking: the text explicitly says the generalization gap still increases with batch size.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Train with label smoothing, mixup, data augmentation, or SAM; compare generalization gap, sharpness, and Jacobian norm.

conditions.value: label smoothing, mixup, data augmentation, or sharpness-aware minimization

rows.baseline: Figure-only; regularization parameters vary by method.
rows.value: The paper reports that sharpness is regularized only in SAM; the relationship between sharpness and generalization varies across strategies.
rows.uncertainty: Five trials; figures report mean and one standard deviation for the extended experiments.
rows.locator: Figure 5; Section 6, “Other regularisation techniques”; Appendix B.3
rows.note: The authors say Jacobian norm is better correlated with generalization gap than Hessian sharpness across the studied strategies. Plot values are figure-only.
rows.check: These regularization comparisons measure ordinary Hessian sharpness, not V7's magnitude-aware measure. None compares dropout conditions for V6. Split the aggregate row by regularization strategy and measured outcome if retained.

rows.subject: ResNet18 and VGG11
rows.operation_detail: Vary label smoothing, mixup, data augmentation, or SAM and measure final metrics.

conditions.value: label smoothing, mixup, data augmentation, or SAM

rows.value: The paper reports that Jacobian norm correlates with generalization gap, while Hessian sharpness is often uncorrelated; all tested strategies initially regularize Jacobian norm, and only SAM regularizes sharpness.
rows.note: Aggregate textual report across the stated datasets, architectures, and batch-normalization settings; individual plot values are figure-only.
rows.check: The aggregate combines datasets, architectures, normalization choices and regularizers, and overlaps R4. These comparisons do not measure a supplied version; they should be separated if retained as evidence for another claim.

rows.subject: VGG11
rows.operation_detail: Train with SGD under varying label smoothing; report sharpness and Jacobian norm during training.
rows.value: Smoother labels are associated with less severe increase in Jacobian norm and sharpness during training.
rows.uncertainty: Five trials; mean and standard deviation plotted.
rows.locator: Appendix B.1; Figures 6–11; Appendix C.1, Figures 28–29
rows.note: The text reports that the relationship changes over the full 90-epoch run: with unsmoothed labels, sharpness ultimately collapses to zero while smoothed-label sharpness plateaus at nonzero values.
rows.check: Conflates distinct experiments. Appendix B.1 uses full-batch gradient descent, with duration set by the unsmoothed model reaching 99% training accuracy; Appendix C.1 uses minibatch SGD over 90 epochs. Learning rates 0.08, 0.04 and 0.02 belong to B.1. These sharpness/Jacobian trajectories do not measure any supplied version.
